parole.testo: From Latin -ista, from Ancient Greek -ιστής (-istḗs).
First attested in the 17th century. Borrowed from Latin -ismus, from Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós, “-ismos”).

parole.significato: abacus (an instrument for performing arithmetical calculations by balls sliding on wires)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abacus (“sideboard; counting board”), from Ancient Greek ἄβαξ (ábax, “board”), possibly from Hebrew אבק (āvāq, “dust”).

parole.significato: academy (a society of learned people united for the advancement of the arts and sciences, and literature, or some parti…
parole.testo: From Latin academia (“academy”), from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδήμια (Akadḗmia, “grove of Akademos”), a place near Athens where Plato taught his school.

parole.significato: alabaster (a fine-grained white or lightly-tinted variety of gypsum, used ornamentally)
parole.testo: From Latin alabastrum, from Ancient Greek ἀλάβαστρον (alábastron, “vessel for ointments made of alabaster”).

parole.significato: alphabetical (according to the sequence of the letters of the alphabet)
parole.testo: From scientific Latin alphabeticus, from Ancient Greek ἄλφα (álpha) and βῆτα (bêta), the names of the first two letters of the Greek alphabet. With -ikus ending.
Borrowed from Latin allegoricus, from Ancient Greek ἀλληγορικός (allēgorikós). With -ikus ending.
From Latin allēgoria, from Ancient Greek ἀλληγορία (allēgoría), from ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + ἀγορεύω (agoreúō, “to speak in assembly”).
Borrowed from Latin aloē (“aloe”), from Ancient Greek ἀλόη (alóē, “aloe”), from Hebrew אֲהָלִים (ʾăhālîm), ultimately from Tamil அகில் (akil).

parole.significato: Amazon (a member of a mythical race of female warriors)
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek Ἀμαζών (Amazṓn).
From Latin amphitheatrum, from Ancient Greek ἀμφιθέατρον (amphithéatron, “amphitheatre”), from ἀμφί- (amphí-, “on both sides”) + θέατρον (théatron, “theatre”, literally “place for viewing”).

parole.significato: amnesty (act of the sovereign power granting oblivion, or a general pardon, for a past offense)
parole.testo: From Latin amnestia, from Ancient Greek ἀμνηστία (amnēstía).
From Latin amnesia, from Ancient Greek ἀμνησία (amnēsía, “forgetfulness”).

parole.significato: anagram (word or phrase created by rearranging letters from another word or phrase)
parole.testo: From Latin anagramma, from Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “up, back”) + γράμμα (grámma, “letter”).

parole.significato: anachronism (a chronological mistake; the erroneous dating of an event, circumstance, or object)
parole.testo: From Latin anachronismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναχρονισμός (anakhronismós), from ἀνά (aná, “against”) + χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). With -izmus ending.
Borrowed from Latin analyticus, from Ancient Greek ἀναλυτικός (analutikós). With -ikus ending.
From Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογίᾱ (analogíā).

parole.significato: anarchy (the state of a society being without authorities or an authoritative governing body)
parole.testo: From Latin anarchia, from Ancient Greek ἀναρχία (anarkhía), from ἀν- (an-, “not”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “power, authority”).
From Latin anaesthesia, from Ancient Greek ἀναισθησία (anaisthēsía), from ἀν- (an-, “not”) with αἴσθησις (aísthēsis, “sensation”).
From Latin anomalia, from Ancient Greek ἀνωμαλία (anōmalía, “anomaly”), from ἀνώμαλος (anṓmalos, “uneven, irregular”), from ἀν- (an-, “not”) + ὠμαλος (ōmalos, “even”).

parole.significato: antibiotic (any substance that can destroy or inhibit the growth of bacteria and similar microorganisms)
parole.testo: From Latin antibioticum, from Ancient Greek βιωτικός (biōtikós, “concerning or relating to life”), from βίος (bíos, “life”).
From Latin antipathia, from Ancient Greek ἀντιπάθεια (antipátheia, “antipathy”).

parole.significato: anthology (a collection of literary works, such as poems or short stories)
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek ἀνθολογία (anthología, “flower-gathering”), from ἀνθολογέω (anthologéō, “I gather flowers”), from ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”) + λέγω (légō, “I gather, pick up, collect”). With -lógia ending.
From Latin apocalypsis, from Ancient Greek ἀποκάλυψις (apokálupsis, “revelation”, literally “uncovering”).

parole.significato: apse, apsis (a recess or projection, with a dome or vault, at the east end of a church)
parole.testo: From Latin apsis (“arch, vault”), from Ancient Greek ἁψίς (hapsís, “arch, vault”).

parole.significato: apathy, disinterest (lack of emotion or motivation; lack of interest or enthusiasm towards something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apathia, from Ancient Greek ἀπάθεια (apátheia, “insensibility, freedom from emotion”).
From scientific Latin archaeologia, from Ancient Greek ἀρχαῖος (arkhaîos, “ancient”), from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “beginning”). With -lógia ending.

parole.significato: archive (a place for storing earlier, and often historical, material)
parole.testo: From Latin archīvum, from Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon, “town hall”).
From Latin arōma (“spice, herb”), from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma, “spice, herb”).

parole.significato: artery (efferent blood vessel from the heart)
parole.testo: From Latin arteria, from Ancient Greek ἀρτηρία (artēría). With -éria ending.

parole.significato: asymptote (a straight line which a curve approaches arbitrarily closely as it goes to infinity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin asymptōta, from Ancient Greek ἀσύμπτωτος (asúmptōtos, “not falling together”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + συν- (sun-, “together”) + πτωτός (ptōtós, “fallen”).
From Latin asthma, from Ancient Greek ἆσθμα (âsthma, “panting”).
From Latin astrologia, from Ancient Greek ἀστρολογία (astrología, “astrology”). See also asztro-. With -lógia ending.

parole.significato: astronomy (the study of the physical universe beyond the Earth's atmosphere)
parole.testo: From the Latin astronomia, from the Ancient Greek ἀστρονομία (astronomía, “astronomy”), from ἄστρον (ástron, “star”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”).
From the Latin athleta, from the Ancient Greek ἀθλητής (athlētḗs, “contestant”). First attested in 1636.

parole.significato: hall, auditorium (a large room at a university for ceremonial gatherings and meetings)
parole.testo: From Latin aula (“forecourt”), from Ancient Greek αὐλή (aulḗ, “courtyard”).

parole.significato: aulic, courtly (pertaining to or befitting of a royal court), especially in sentiment or behaviour
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aulicus (“princely”), from Ancient Greek αὐλῐκός (aulĭkós, “of the court”). With -ikus ending. First attested in 1787. Doublet of aula.

parole.significato: authentic (conforming to reality and therefore worthy of trust, reliance, or belief)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin authenticus, from Ancient Greek αὐθεντικός (authentikós, “principal, genuine”). With -ikus ending.
From scientific Latin autismus, from Ancient Greek αὐτός (autós, “self”). With -izmus ending.

parole.significato: axon (a nerve fibre which is a long slender projection of a nerve cell, and which conducts nerve impulses away from the…
parole.testo: From scientific Latin axon, from Ancient Greek ἄξων (áxōn, “axis”).

From scientific Latin biologia, from Ancient Greek βίος (bíos, “life”). With -lógia ending.

parole.significato: botany (scientific study of plants, a branch of biology)
parole.testo: From scientific Latin botanica (scientia), from Ancient Greek βοτανικός (botanikós).

From Latin coemētērium, from Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion), from κοιμάω (koimáō, “to put to sleep”).

parole.significato: cistern (a waterproof below-ground receptacle for holding liquids, usually rain water)

parole.significato: diagnostician (a person who diagnoses, especially a medical doctor)
parole.testo: From scientific Latin diagnosta, from Ancient Greek διαγνώστες (diagnṓstes).
From scientific Latin diagnostica, from Ancient Greek διαγνωστικός (diagnōstikós). With -ika ending.

parole.significato: diagnosis (identification of the nature and cause of an illness)
parole.testo: From Latin diagnōsis, from Ancient Greek διάγνωσις (diágnōsis). With -ózis ending.
From Latin diagramma, from Ancient Greek διάγραμμα (diágramma).

parole.significato: diacritical (capable of distinguishing or of making a distinction)
parole.testo: From scientific Latin diacriticus, from Ancient Greek διακριτικός (diakritikós, “distinguishing, separative”), from διακρῑ́νω (diakrī́nō, “to distinguish, separate”), from δια- (dia-, “between”) + κρῑ́νω (krī́nō, “to separate, distinguish”). With -ikus ending.

parole.significato: dynasty (a series of rulers or dynasts from one family)

From scientific Latin dyslexia, from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-) expressing the idea of difficulty, and λέξις (léxis, “diction”, “word”).

parole.significato: dysentery (a disease characterised by inflammation of the intestines)
parole.testo: From Latin dysenteria, from Ancient Greek δυσεντερία (dusentería), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + ἔντερα (éntera, “bowels”). With -éria ending.

parole.significato: diet (a controlled regimen of food and drink, as to influence health)
parole.testo: Internationalism, from Latin diaeta (“diet, regimen”), from Ancient Greek δῐ́αιτᾰ (dĭ́aită, “way of living, living space; decision, judgement”).

parole.significato: ectoplasm (the outer granule-free layer of cytoplasm)

parole.significato: energy (the quantitative property that must be transferred to an object in order to perform work on, or to heat, the ob…
parole.testo: First attested in 1627. Borrowed from Latin energia, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia).
From scientific Latin entomologia, from Ancient Greek ἔντομον (éntomon, “insect”). With -lógia ending.
From scientific Latin epidemiologia, from Latin epidēmia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδημία (epidēmía). With -lógia ending.

parole.significato: epilepsy (a medical condition in which the sufferer experiences seizures or convulsions and blackouts)
parole.testo: From scientific Latin epilepsia (“epilepsy”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιληψία (epilēpsía, “seizure”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + λῆψις (lêpsis, “seizure”), from λαμβάνω (lambánō, “to take hold of”).

parole.significato: epic (extended narrative poem in elevated or dignified language)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epos (“epic”) (compare English epos (obsolete), German Epos), from Ancient Greek ἔπος (épos, “speech, story”).
From scientific Latin erythrocyta, from Ancient Greek ἐρυθρός (eruthrós, “red”) + κύτος (kútos, “vessel, jar”).

parole.significato: etymology (the branch of linguistics that deals with the origin, derivation, and formation of individual words and word…
parole.testo: From scientific Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología), from ἔτυμος (étumos, “real, true, actual”). With -lógia ending.
From Latin ethnicus, from Ancient Greek ἐθνικός (ethnikós), from ἔθνος (éthnos, “tribe, country, nation”).
From scientific Latin euthanasia, from Ancient Greek εὐθανασία (euthanasía), from εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + θάνατος (thánatos, “death”).
From Latin evangelista, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελιστής (euangelistḗs).
Borrowed from Latin evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news”).

parole.testo: From scientific Latin physiologia, from Ancient Greek φυσιολογία (phusiología, “natural philosophy”), from φύσις (phúsis, “nature”). With -lógia ending.

parole.significato: geography (the study of the physical properties of the earth)
parole.testo: From Latin geographia, from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).

parole.significato: geology (the science that studies the structure of the earth)
parole.testo: From scientific Latin geologia, from Ancient Greek γῆ (gê, “earth”) + -λογία (-logía).
Borrowed from Latin geometria, from Ancient Greek γεωμετρία (geōmetría, “geometry, land-survey”).

From scientific Latin gnosticismus, from Ancient Greek γνωστικός (gnōstikós, “of or for knowing, cognitive”). With -izmus ending.

parole.significato: hell (in various religions, the place where some or all spirits are believed to go after death)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gehenna, from Ancient Greek γέεννᾰ (géennă), from Hebrew גֵּיהִנּוֹם (ge'henom).

parole.significato: harmony (two or more notes played simultaneously to produce a chord)
parole.testo: From Latin harmonia, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονία (harmonía, “joint, union, agreement, concord of sounds”).
First attested in 1808. Borrowed from Latin hetaera, from Ancient Greek ἑταίρᾱ (hetaírā), feminine of ἑταῖρος (hetaîros, “companion”).
From Latin hydrophobia, from Ancient Greek ὑδροφοβία (hudrophobía).

parole.significato: hydrate (a solid compound containing or linked to water molecules)
parole.testo: From scientific Latin hydratus (“saturated with water”), from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”).

parole.significato: anthem, national anthem (a choral or vocal composition, often with a religious or political lyric)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hymnus, from Ancient Greek ὕμνος (húmnos).

parole.significato: hypnotic (of, or relating to hypnosis or hypnotism)
parole.testo: From scientific Latin hypnoticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “inclined to sleep, putting to sleep, sleepy”), from ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”). With -ikus ending.
From Latin hypothesis (“hypothesis”), from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, “basis of an argument, supposition”). With -zis ending.

Borrowed from Latin idea, from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”).

parole.significato: idiom (any mode of expression peculiar to a language, person, or group of people)
parole.testo: From Latin idioma (“idiom”), from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “specific property, unique feature”).
Borrowed from Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”, literally “private person”).

parole.significato: icon (a religious painting, often done on wooden panels)
parole.testo: From Latin icon (“image”), from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn, “likeness, image, portrait”).

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter Y/y.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ypsilon, from Ancient Greek ὖ ψιλόν (û psilón).

parole.significato: school (an institution dedicated to teaching and learning)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin schola (“lecture, school, sect”), from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ, “leisure, free time, disputation, school”).

parole.significato: iota, jot (a very small, insignificant quantity)
parole.testo: From Latin iota, from Ancient Greek ἰῶτα (iôta).

parole.significato: hyacinth (any bulbous plant of the genus Hyacinthus)
parole.testo: First attested in 1416. Borrowed from Latin hyacinthus, from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos, “any of several dark blue flowers”).
From Latin canālis, from canna (“reed, cane”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”).

parole.significato: cardiology (the study of the structure, function, and disorders of the heart)
parole.testo: From scientific Latin cardiologia, from Ancient Greek καρδία (kardía, “heart”) + -λογία (-logía, “the study of”).

Borrowed from Latin catholicus, from Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós), from κατά (katá, “according to”) + ὅλος (hólos, “whole”). With -ikus ending.

parole.significato: cenotaph (an empty tomb or a monument erected in honor of a person or group of people whose remains are elsewhere)
parole.testo: From Latin cenotaphium, from Ancient Greek κενοτάφιον (kenotáphion, “empty tomb”), from κενός (kenós, “empty”) + τάφος (táphos, “tomb”).
From Latin chirurgus (“surgeon”), from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós, “surgeon”), from χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”).
From scientific Latin climax, from Ancient Greek κλῖμαξ (klîmax, “ladder, staircase, [rhetorical] climax”), from κλίνω (klínō, “to lean, slant”).
From Latin and Ancient Greek. With -ális ending.
From Latin clima (“region, slope of the Earth”), from Ancient Greek κλίμα (klíma, “region, zone of latitude”, originally “slope”), from κλίνω (klínō, “to slope, incline”).

parole.significato: cholera (an infectious disease of humans and domestic animals)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cholera, from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra).

From Latin criterium, from Ancient Greek κριτήριον (kritḗrion).
Borrowed from Latin crocodilus, from Ancient Greek κροκόδειλος (krokódeilos). Via German Krokodil is also a possibility.

parole.significato: crater (the basin-like opening or mouth of a volcano)
parole.testo: From Latin crater, from Ancient Greek κρᾱτήρ (krātḗr, “mixingbowl, wassail-bowl”).

From scientific Latin crisis, from Ancient Greek κρίσις (krísis, “a separating, power of distinguishing, decision, choice, election, judgment, dispute”), from κρίνω (krínō, “pick out, choose, decide, judge”). With -zis ending.
Borrowed from Latin chronicus, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “of time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). With -ikus ending.
From Latin chorus, from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós, “circle dance, band of singers and dancers, place for dancing”).

A wanderword introduced into Hungarian possibly via German but a West Slavic borrowing cannot be excluded. Compare German Kümmel, Greek κύμινο (kýmino), from Latin cuminum, from Ancient Greek κύμινον (kúminon).

Internationalism, analogous to English commonplace, German Gemeinplatz, French lieu commun etc. Calque of Latin locus commūnis, from Ancient Greek κοινὸς τόπος (koinòs tópos). Equivalent to köz (“public, general, common”) + hely (“place”).
From Latin labyrinthus (“maze”), from Ancient Greek λαβύρινθος (labúrinthos, “maze”).

parole.significato: laconic (using as few words as possible; pithy and concise)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Lacōnicus (“Spartan”), from Ancient Greek Λακωνικός (Lakōnikós, “Laconian”). Laconia was the region inhabited and ruled by the Spartans, who were known for their brevity in speech. With -ikus ending.
From scientific Latin leucocyta, from Ancient Greek λευκός (leukós, “white”) + κύτος (kútos, “vessel, jar”).

parole.significato: lily (any of several flowers in the genus Lilium)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin līlium (“lily”), from Ancient Greek λείριον (leírion).

From Latin liturgia, from Ancient Greek λειτουργία (leitourgía), from λειτ- (leit-), from λαός (laós, “people”) + -ουργός (-ourgós), from ἔργον (érgon, “work”) (the public work of the people done on behalf of the people).
Borrowed from Latin lampas (“torch”), from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “torch”), from λάμπω (lámpō, “to shine, give light”).
From Latin lithium, from Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”).
From Latin mathēmatica (“mathematics”), from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós, “fond of learning”), from μάθημα (máthēma, “knowledge, study, learning”).

parole.significato: mausoleum (a large stately tomb or a building housing such a tomb)
parole.testo: First attested in 1604. Borrowed from Latin mausōlēum (“mausoleum”), from Ancient Greek Μαύσωλος (Maúsōlos). Named for Mausolus (Μαύσωλος or Μαύσσωλλος), satrap of the Persian empire and ruler of Caria.
Borrowed from Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós, “atrabilious, impulsive, of atrabilious or melancholic temperament”). With -ikus ending.

parole.significato: mint (any plant in the genus Mentha in the family Lamiaceae)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin menta, from Ancient Greek μίνθη (mínthē).
From Latin metaphora, from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá), from μεταφέρω (metaphérō, “to transfer, apply”), from μετά (metá, “with, across, after”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”).

parole.significato: myrrh (dried sap of the myrrha tree)
parole.testo: From Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρα (múrrha), of Semitic origin.

parole.significato: myrtle (evergreen shrub or small tree of the genus Myrtus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin myrtus (“myrtle”), from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos, “myrtle”). First attested in 1533.

parole.significato: mystic, mystical (of or relating to mystics, mysticism or occult mysteries)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mysticus, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós, “secret, mystic”), from μύστης (mústēs, “one who has been initiated”).

parole.significato: mystery (something secret or unexplainable; an unknown)
parole.testo: From Latin mysterium, from Ancient Greek μῠστήρῐον (mŭstḗrĭon).
From scientific Latin mitochondrium, from Ancient Greek μίτος (mítos, “thread”) + χονδρίον (khondríon), diminutive of χόνδρος (khóndros, “grain, morsel”).

parole.significato: mitosis (the division of a cell nucleus in which the genome is copied and separated into two identical halves; it is no…
parole.testo: From scientific Latin mitosis, from Ancient Greek μίτος (mítos, “thread”) + -osis, probably in reference to the thread-like chromatin seen during mitosis.
First attested in 1578. Borrowed from Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs, “monarch, ruler”).
From Latin monarchia (“monarchy”), from Ancient Greek μοναρχίᾱ (monarkhíā, “absolute rule”), from μόνος (mónos, “alone”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “ruler, leader”).
From Latin monopolium, from Ancient Greek μονοπώλιον (monopṓlion, “a right of exclusive sale”), from μόνος (mónos, “sole”) + πωλέω (pōléō, “to barter, sell”).
Borrowed from Latin monastērium, from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, “hermit's cell”), from μόνος (mónos, “alone”).
From Latin mūsica, from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ, “of a Muse”), derived from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”).
Borrowed from Latin magicus, from Ancient Greek μαγικός (magikós, “magical”). With -ikus ending.

parole.significato: magnet (a piece of material that attracts some metals by magnetism)
parole.testo: From scientific Latin magnes, from Ancient Greek μαγνήτης λίθος (magnḗtēs líthos, “Magnesian stone”).
From Latin magus, from Ancient Greek μάγος (mágos, “magician”).
Borrowed from Latin mania, from Ancient Greek μανία (manía). First attested in 1791.
From Latin martyr, from Ancient Greek μάρτυρ (mártur, “martyr”), later form of μάρτυς (mártus, “witness”).

parole.significato: Moorish (of or relating to the Moors or their culture)
parole.testo: From Latin Maurus (“a Moor, meaning a Mauritanian, an inhabitant of Mauritania”), from Ancient Greek Μαῦρος (Maûros), also via German Mohr.

parole.significato: Muse (one of the nine Ancient Greek deities of the arts)
parole.testo: From Latin Musa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).
From Latin nānus (“dwarf”), from Ancient Greek νᾶνος (nânos).
Borrowed from Latin narcoticus, from Ancient Greek ναρκωτικός (narkōtikós, “numbing”). With -ikus ending.
From scientific Latin neodymium, from neo- + didymium, from Ancient Greek δίδυμος (dídumos, “twin”) + -ium (suffix denoting chemical elements).
From Latin nomades (“roaming shepherds”), from Ancient Greek νομάς (nomás, “roaming about for pasture”).
From Latin oligarchia (“oligarchy”), from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχία (oligarkhía, “rule of the few”), from ὀλίγος (olígos, “few”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “ruler, leader”).
Borrowed from Latin oncologia, from Ancient Greek ὄγκος (ónkos, “lump, mass, bulk”) + -λογία (-logía, “study of”). With -lógia ending.
Borrowed from Latin organicus, from Ancient Greek ὀργανικός (organikós). With -ikus ending.
From scientific Latin orthopaedia (“orthopaedics”), from Ancient Greek ὀρθός (orthós, “straight, right, true”) + παιδεία (paideía, “rearing of children, education”), from παῖς (paîs, “child”).

parole.significato: pandemic (disease that affects a wide geographical area and a large proportion of the population)
parole.testo: From scientific Latin pandemia (“affecting all the people”), from Ancient Greek πάνδημος (pándēmos, “of or belonging to all the people, public”).
First attested in 1508. Borrowed from Latin papyrus (“papyrus”), from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros).

parole.significato: papyrus (a plant Cyperus papyrus in the sedge family, native to the Nile river valley)
parole.testo: From Latin papȳrus, from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros, “papyrus”).

From Latin paradīsum, accusative singular of paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos, “park, paradise, Garden of Eden”), from an Iranian source, compare Avestan 𐬞𐬀𐬌𐬭𐬌⸱𐬛𐬀𐬉𐬰𐬀 (paⁱri.daēza, “walled enclusure, encompassing”), compound of 𐬞𐬀𐬌𐬭𐬌 (paⁱri, “around”) + 𐬛𐬀𐬉𐬰𐬀 (daēza, “wall”).
From Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis, “palsy”), from παραλύω (paralúō, “to disable on one side”), from παρα- (para-, “beside”) + λύω (lúō, “loosen”). With -zis ending.
From Latin parodia, from Ancient Greek παρῳδία (parōidía, “parody”).
From Latin apothēca, from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “storehouse”).

parole.significato: pedagogue, educator (someone specialized in education as a profession in general)
parole.testo: From Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós, “a slave who accompanied a child to and from school”), later ("a teacher"), from παῖς (paîs, “child”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”).

parole.significato: periphery, outskirts (outside boundary, parts or surface)
parole.testo: From scientific Latin peripherīa, from Ancient Greek περιφέρεια (periphéreia, “circumference, periphery”). With -éria ending.

parole.significato: period (period of time seen as a single coherent entity)
parole.testo: From Latin periodus, from Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos).

parole.significato: Persian (of or relating to Persia/Persis or its people)
parole.testo: From Latin Persa, from Ancient Greek Πέρσης (Pérsēs, “a Persian”).

parole.significato: pyramid (ancient construction with a square or rectangular base and four triangular sides)
parole.testo: From Latin pyramis, from Ancient Greek πυραμίς (puramís, “pyramid”), perhaps from Egyptian.

From scientific Latin python, from Ancient Greek Πύθων (Púthōn), the name of the mythological enormous serpent at Delphi slain by Apollo, from Πῡθώ (Pūthṓ), the early name of Delphi, from πύθω (púthō, “to rot, to decay”).
From Latin planeta, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer”), from πλανάω (planáō, “wander about, stray”).
From scientific Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós), from πλεονάζω (pleonázō, “to be superfluous”), from πλείων (pleíōn, “more”).
From Latin politica, from Ancient Greek πολιτική (politikḗ, “politics”).
Borrowed from Latin polīticus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós, “of citizens or the state”). With -ikus ending.
From Latin poema, from Ancient Greek ποίημα (poíēma), from ποιέω (poiéō).
From Latin poēta (“poet”), from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs, “poet, author”), from ποιέω (poiéō, to make) + -της (-tēs, “-er”, masculine agentive suffix).

Borrowed from Latin pragmaticus, from Ancient Greek πραγματικός (pragmatikós, “active, versed in affairs”), from πρᾶγμα (prâgma, “a thing done, a fact”), in plural πράγματα (prágmata, “affairs, state affairs, public business, etc.”), from πράσσειν (prássein, “to do”). With -ikus ending.
Borrowed from Latin practicus, from Ancient Greek πρακτικός (praktikós). With -ikus ending.

parole.significato: prism (transparent block with triangular ends used to split light)
parole.testo: From Latin prisma, from Ancient Greek πρῖσμα (prîsma).

From Latin problema, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, “anything thrown forward, hindrance, obstacle, anything projecting, a headland, promontory”), from προβάλλω (probállō, “to throw or lay something in front of someone, to put forward”), from προ- (pro-, “in front of”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to thr

parole.significato: prognosis (forecast of the future course of a disease or disorder, based on medical knowledge)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prognōsis, from Ancient Greek πρόγνωσις (prógnōsis, “foreknowledge, perceiving beforehand, prediction”), from prefix προ- (pro-, “before”) + γνῶσις (gnôsis, “inquiry, investigation, knowing”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “know”). With -ózis ending.

parole.significato: prologue (a section used as an introduction in a play or a novel)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prologus, from Ancient Greek πρόλογος (prólogos).
From Latin prophētīa, from Ancient Greek προφητεία (prophēteía, “prophecy”).
From Latin prophēta (“prophet”), from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs, “spokesman”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + φάναι (phánai, “to speak”).

From Latin pardus, from Ancient Greek πάρδος (párdos, “male panther”), from the same source (probably Iranian) as Sanskrit पृदाकु (pṛ́dāku, “panther, tiger, snake”) and Persian پلنگ (palang, “panther”).

parole.significato: platform (a raised stage from which speeches are made and songs are sung)
parole.testo: From Latin podium, from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “base”), from diminutive of πούς (poús, “foot”).
From Latin rabbi, from Ancient Greek ῥαββί (rhabbí), from Hebrew רַבִּי (rabí).
From the Latin rhinoceros, from the Ancient Greek ῥινόκερως (rhinókerōs, “rhinoceros”), coined from ρίς (rís, “nose”) + κέρας (kéras, “horn”).
Borrowed from Latin rosa (“rose”), itself of uncertain origin, perhaps from Ancient Greek ῥόδον (rhódon).
Borrowed from Latin scorpio, from Ancient Greek σκόρπιος (skórpios, “scorpion”). With -ió ending.
From Latin sperma, from Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma, “seed, semen”).
Borrowed from Latin spongia (“sponge”), from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá).
Borrowed from Latin stropha, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στροφή (strophḗ, “a turn, bend, twist”).

parole.significato: stage, phase, state (a period considered at a certain time in a process or development)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stadium, from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion)

parole.significato: stole (a long, wide scarf-like garment worn about the shoulders)
parole.testo: From Latin stola (“robe, vestment”), from Ancient Greek στολή (stolḗ, “garment, equipment”).

parole.significato: salamander (a long, slender, chiefly terrestrial amphibian of the order Caudata)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin salamandra, from Ancient Greek σαλαμάνδρα (salamándra).

parole.significato: sandal (a type of open shoe made up of straps or bands holding a sole to the foot)
parole.testo: A wanderword. Via multiple borrowing. Compare German Sandale, French sandale, Italian sandalo. Ultimately from Latin sandalium, from Ancient Greek σανδάλιον (sandálion), diminutive of σάνδαλον (sándalon, “sandal”).

parole.significato: sepsis (a serious medical condition in which the whole body is inflamed, causing injury to its own tissues and organs a…
parole.testo: From scientific Latin sepsis, from Ancient Greek σῆψις (sêpsis, “putrefaction”).
From Latin syllogismus, from Ancient Greek συλλογισμός (sullogismós, “inference, conclusion”). With -izmus ending.

From Latin symbolum (“sign, mark”), from Ancient Greek σύμβολον (súmbolon, “token, watchword”), from συμβάλλω (sumbállō, “to throw together, correspond”), from σύν (sún, “together”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”).

parole.significato: symmetry (correspondence on either side of a dividing line, plane, center, or axis)
parole.testo: From Latin symmetria, from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría).

parole.significato: symptom (a perceived change in some function, sensation or appearance of a person that indicates a disease or disorder,…
parole.testo: From scientific Latin symptoma, from Ancient Greek σύμπτωμα (súmptōma, “a happening, accident, symptom of disease”), from stem of συμπίπτω (sumpíptō, “Ι befall”), from συν- (sun-, “together”) + πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”).
Borrowed from Latin sympathia, from Ancient Greek σῠμπᾰ́θειᾰ (sŭmpắtheiă, “fellow feeling”)

parole.significato: syndrome (recognizable pattern of symptoms of an illness)
parole.testo: From scientific Latin syndroma, from Ancient Greek συνδρομή (sundromḗ, “concurrence of symptoms, concourse”), from σύνδρομος (súndromos, “running together”), from συν- (sun-, “with”) + δρόμος (drómos, “running, course”).

From Latin synthesis, from Ancient Greek σύνθεσις (súnthesis, “a putting together; composition”), from συντίθημι (suntíthēmi, “put together, combine”), from σύν (sún, “together”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “set, place”). With -zis ending.
Borrowed from Latin systema, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma, “organised whole, body”), from σύν (sún, “with, together”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).

parole.significato: Scythian (of or relating to Scythia or the Scythians)
parole.testo: From Latin Scytha (“Scythian”), from Ancient Greek Σκύθης (Skúthēs, “Scythian”).
From Latin sēpia, from Ancient Greek σηπία (sēpía, “cuttlefish”).
From Latin Satān, from Ancient Greek Σατάν (Satán), from Hebrew שָׂטָן (Śāṭān, “adversary, accuser”).

parole.significato: tactics (the military science that deals with achieving the objectives set by strategy)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tactica, from Ancient Greek τακτικὴ τέχνη (taktikḕ tékhnē, “art of arrangement”), from τάσσω (tássō, “arrange”). First attested in 1788.

parole.significato: taxis (the directional movement of an organism in response to a stimulus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin taxis, from Ancient Greek τάξις (táxis, “arrangement, order”).
From scientific Latin theoreticus, from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός (theōrētikós, “contemplative, speculative”). With -ikus ending.
From Latin therapeuta (“therapist”), from Ancient Greek θεραπευτής (therapeutḗs, “one who waits on another, an attendant”), from θεραπεύω (therapeúō, “to wait on, attend, serve, cure”).
From Latin therapia, from Ancient Greek θεραπεία (therapeía, “service, medical treatment”).
Borrowed from Latin tiāra, from Ancient Greek τιάρα (tiára).

parole.significato: tiger (Panthera tigris, a large predatory mammal of the cat family)
parole.testo: From Latin tigris, from Ancient Greek τίγρις (tígris, “tiger”), probably of Iranian origin.
From Latin Titan, from Ancient Greek Τιτάν (Titán).
From scientific Latin topologia, from Ancient Greek τόπος (tópos, “place, locality”). With -lógia (“study of, a branch of knowledge”) ending.
From Latin thorax, from Ancient Greek θώραξ (thṓrax, “breastplate, chest”), created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries.
Borrowed from Latin tragicus, from Ancient Greek τραγικός (tragikós, “of or relating to tragedy”). With -ikus ending.

From Latin tragoedia, from Ancient Greek τραγῳδία (tragōidía, “epic play, tragedy”), from τράγος (trágos, “male goat”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”), a reference to the goat-satyrs of the theatrical plays of the Dorians.

parole.significato: trigonometry (the branch of mathematics that deals with the relationships between the sides and the angles of triangles…
parole.testo: From scientific Latin trigonometria, from Ancient Greek τρίγωνον (trígōnon, “triangle”) + -metria (“-metry”).

parole.significato: tropics (region of the Earth lying between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tropus (“figure of speech, trope”), from Ancient Greek τρόπος (trópos, “turn; figure of speech; musical mode”). The “tropics” sense (etymology 1 sense 1) is possibly a semantic loan from German Tropen (“tropics”). The phonetic form was probably influenced by trópus (“trope”), whi

parole.significato: trope (a figure of speech in which words or phrases are used with a nonliteral or figurative meaning)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tropus (“figure of speech, trope”), from Ancient Greek τρόπος (trópos, “turn; figure of speech; musical mode”). First attested in 1763.
Borrowed from Latin thema, from Ancient Greek θέμα (théma).
From Latin typus, from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark, impression, type”), from τύπτω (túptō, “to strike, beat”).
Borrowed from Latin tonus, from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos).
From scientific Latin zygota, from Ancient Greek ζυγωτός (zugōtós, “yoked”), past participle of ζυγόω (zugóō, “to yoke”), from ζυγόν (zugón, “yoke”).

parole.significato: zodiac (the belt-like region of the celestial sphere corresponding to the apparent path of the sun over the course of a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin zodiacus, from Ancient Greek ζῳδῐᾰκός (zōidĭăkós) κύκλος (kúklos, “little animal cycle”).
From the Latin synagoga (“Jewish congregation”), from the Ancient Greek συναγωγή (sunagōgḗ, “assembly”), from συνάγειν (sunágein, “to assemble”).

parole.significato: synod (an ecclesiastic council or meeting to consult on church matters)
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1519. Borrowed from Latin synodus, from Ancient Greek σύνοδος (súnodos, “assembly, meeting”), from σύν (sún, “with”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way, path”).

parole.significato: iris (plant of the genus Iris having attractive blooms)
parole.testo: From Latin īris, from Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris, “rainbow”).
Borrowed from Latin opium, from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion), from ὀπός (opós, “juice of a plant”).
From Latin hōra (“hour”), from Ancient Greek ὥρᾱ (hṓrā, “any limited time”).
